nameStory: The angel wing clam gets its heavenly name from its pure white, translucent shells that spread apart like delicate angel wings when viewed from above. When the shells are open and catching light underwater, they create an ethereal, wing-like silhouette that early naturalists found irresistibly angelic.
description: The angel wing is a large, white bivalve clam that lives buried deep in sandy and muddy seafloors along New England's coast. Its two shells are thin, translucent, and ribbed, appearing almost ghostly white when cleaned. These clams can grow quite large, with shells reaching several inches in length, and they're known for their ability to bore deep burrows into soft sediments.

idTips.label: Shell appearance
idTips.description: Pure white to translucent shells with prominent ridged ribs running from the hinge to the outer edge, feeling rough and textured like a washboard when you run your finger across them

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Elongated oval shells that gape open at both ends even when the clam tries to close, giving them their distinctive wing-like appearance

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large clams that can span 4-6 inches in length, much bigger than most common beach clams you'll find

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Shells feel surprisingly thin and fragile, almost papery compared to thick-shelled clams like quahogs, and may be slightly chalky to the touch

idTips.label: Beach finds
idTips.description: Usually found as single valves (half-shells) washed up on beaches, rarely as complete specimens due to their fragile nature and deep-burrowing lifestyle

habitat: Angel wings live in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, burrowing 3-8 feet deep into soft sandy and muddy bottoms in protected bays, estuaries, and nearshore areas. They prefer areas with gentle currents and fine sediments where they can slowly drill their burrows over many years. You'll most likely encounter their shells washed up on sandy beaches after storms rather than finding the living clams themselves.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms and ice-out, appearing bright white and less weathered than winter finds.
seasonality.summer: Peak beachcombing season for finding angel wing shells on sandy beaches, especially after summer storms that disturb the offshore populations.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms frequently bring shells ashore, often mixed with other deep-water species that get churned up from offshore beds.
seasonality.winter: Winter beach-walking may reveal weathered shells from previous seasons, though they'll be more worn and chalky-looking from months of wave action.

funFact: Angel wing clams are nature's living drill bits - they spend years slowly rotating their shells like a boring machine to carve perfectly round burrows up to 8 feet deep into the seafloor, using the ridges on their shells as cutting tools!
confusionNotes: Angel wings are most commonly confused with razor clam shells, but angel wings are much whiter, more fragile, and have prominent ridged ribs, while razor clams are yellowish, smoother, and much more rectangular. Remember: angel wings have "heavenly ridges," razor clams are "smooth as a blade."
contextualKnowledge: Despite their delicate appearance, angel wings are actually in the piddock family - clams that specialize in boring into hard surfaces. The name "piddock" comes from an old English word meaning "to make small holes," reflecting their drilling abilities.
compareHints: Angel wings are the only member of their genus in New England waters, making them unique among local piddocks. Compared to other boring clams in the piddock family, angel wings are much larger, more translucent, and have more pronounced ribbing on their shells. Other piddocks in the region tend to be smaller, darker, and bore into harder substrates like wood or rock rather than soft sediments.
